## "Entropy measure" across the corpus

The phrase is used in two distinct senses in these papers. The most complete treatment of *entropy measures* as a family of information-theoretic quantities is in **0709.2178.pdf** (a paper applying entropy concepts to stock-market volatility). A second, applied sense — *relative entropy* as a regularizer/distance — appears in **2607.08291.pdf**.

### 1. Entropy as a measure of uncertainty/disorder — the core definition (0709.2178.pdf)

The paper introduces entropy as a physical measure and then its information-theoretic generalizations:

- **Origin and meaning.** Entropy was introduced by Clausius (1865) in thermodynamics; the most common reading in the literature is as **"a measure of ignorance, disorder, uncertainty or even lack of information."** Shannon later showed it applies "in any context where probabilities can be defined," so thermodynamic entropy is a special case of Shannon entropy (0709.2178.pdf, p. 3).

- **Shannon entropy** (the canonical entropy measure), for a discrete random variable X with distribution pᵢ (p. 4, Eq. 7):

  S(X) = −Σᵢ pᵢ ln pᵢ

  Properties given on p. 4: it is zero when the system produces only one event (no uncertainty), increases with the number of equally-likely events, and is **maximal when all outcomes are equally probable**. For a *continuous* variable the entropy can be negative (the measurement scale fixes an arbitrary zero at the uniform distribution over a unit volume).

- **Rényi entropy** — a generalization replacing linear averaging with the Kolmogorov–Nagumo (quasi-linear) mean plus additivity (p. 4, Eq. 8):

  Sₐ(X) = 1/(1−α) · ln( Σᵢ pᵢ^α ),  for α > 0, α ≠ 1

  In the limit α → 1 it reduces to Shannon entropy. Csiszár later interpreted the α index as the cutoff rate for hypothesis-testing problems (p. 5).

- **Tsallis entropy** (a.k.a. Havrda–Charvát–Daróczy–Tsallis entropy) — designed for systems with long-range interactions and multifractal structure (p. 5, Eq. 9):

  S_q(X) = (1 − Σᵢ pᵢ^q) / (q − 1)

  It recovers Shannon entropy as q → 1; q < 1 privileges rare events and q > 1 privileges common events. Shannon entropy yields exponential equilibrium distributions whereas Tsallis entropy yields **power-law** distributions; for finite variance q must lie in 1 ≤ q < 5/3 (p. 5).

This paper is the corpus's clearest, self-contained answer to "what is an entropy measure": Shannon, Rényi, and Tsallis are three such measures, all quantifying uncertainty over a probability distribution.

### 2. Relative entropy as an applied measure (2607.08291.pdf, p. 10)

In *"Robustness in Sequential Decision Making under Evolving Uncertainty,"* entropy appears as **relative entropy (Kullback–Leibler divergence)** used to regularize optimal transport. In the entropically-regularized ("Sinkhorn") transport cost

Wδ(P₁,P₂) = inf_γ [ ∫ c dγ + δ·H(γ | P₁⊗ν) ],

the term **H(γ | P₁⊗ν) is the relative entropy** of the transport plan γ with respect to the product measure P₁⊗ν, defined via the Radon–Nikodym derivative as

H(γ | P₁⊗ν) = E_{(x̃,ỹ)∼γ}[ log( dγ / (dP₁ dν) ) ].

Here the entropy term "penalizes highly concentrated transport plans," encouraging uncertainty to be spread more smoothly across future states; the parameter δ trades off worst-case perturbation against entropic smoothing (2607.08291.pdf, p. 10).

### Other, more incidental appearances

Keyword search shows entropy is used across the corpus in narrower, applied roles rather than as a defined measure:
- **Cross-entropy loss** as a training/evaluation metric in ML papers — e.g. cross-entropy validation loss as the scaling-law quantity (2005.14165.pdf, p. 11; 2206.07682.pdf, p. 19; 1712.00409.pdf, p. 16).
- **Entropy-production estimators** as irreversibility diagnostics in a nonequilibrium world-model paper (2607.02154.pdf, p. 6).
- **Confinement entropy change** ΔS/k_B in a polymer/physics context (0811.0781.pdf, p. 15).
- Image-entropy estimates (nats/image) as a consistency check on scaling-law loss floors (2010.14701.pdf, p. 19).

### Bottom line

If "entropy measure" means the information-theoretic quantity, the definitive answer is **0709.2178.pdf (pp. 3–5)**: entropy is a measure of uncertainty/disorder, with **Shannon** (S = −Σ pᵢ ln pᵢ), **Rényi**, and **Tsallis** entropies as the three principal measures, each generalizing the previous one. For an entropy measure used *as a tool* (a divergence/regularizer), see the **relative entropy** in **2607.08291.pdf (p. 10)**.

*(Note: semantic search was unavailable — fastembed isn't installed — so this is keyword-based coverage; the two primary sources were read in full to confirm the definitions.)*
